prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which magic-wavelength trapping allows many neutral atoms to be interrogated at once with the light shift cancelled, bringing optical frequency standards to the 10^-18 level of accuracy and stability.

statement.case_for: I keep optical lattice clocks (B059) with Katori and Ye. After reading the full first round, the case that survives is narrower than the one I opened with, and I think it is stronger for that. It rests on two things that were demonstrated, not promised: Katori's magic-wavelength condition, which makes a trapped ensemble of neutral atoms behave as if it were free of the trap light shift, and the realisation by Ye's group and others of systematic uncertainty and stability near 1e-18 with thousands of atoms interrogated in parallel. The chair asks what this adds in kind to the 2005 and 2012 prizes. My answer: the comb is a frequency ruler and the ion clock is one quantum system with a statistical limit set by one particle; the lattice clock combines a Lamb-Dicke-confined, recoil-free ensemble with an engineered cancellation of the dominant perturbation, which is a different route to the stability limit and is the reason the 1e-18 regime is reachable in practice. Independent groups in strontium and ytterbium reproduce it, and the use of clock comparisons for geodesy and tests of constants is already happening. I do not rest the case on the redefinition of the second. Attribution is the cleanest on the shortlist: the supplied proposals converge on the same two names, with a clear split between concept and frontier realisation.
statement.case_against: The overlap objection is real and I cannot make it disappear by argument; it can only be contained by a narrow citation that names magic-wavelength lattice trapping and many-atom interrogation. Several colleagues (Mehlig, Eriksson, Olsson, Johansson) read this as a superb refinement of a toolchain already recognised, and a reasonable committee could prefer to reward a new class of matter (B016) over a measurement capability. Other groups, notably SYRTE/Lemonde, PTB and the wider JILA/NIST effort, made milestone contributions to the accuracy record that a two-name credit leaves out, and priority between Katori's proposal and early lattice-clock demonstrations is something I have not checked in the primary papers. Part of the payoff, the redefinition of the second, is still prospective, so waiting is a defensible position even though I do not hold it.

responses.point: Mehlig asks whether B059 is a discovery or a refinement of precision metrology begun with combs and single-ion clocks, and says B016 opened a new conceptual category, while saying he would not oppose B059 as the prize.
responses.response: I accept the distinction between a new category and an improved capability, and I do not claim the lattice clock is a classification of anything. What I would ask is that we not treat 'new category' as the only form of discovery. The magic-wavelength condition is an idea about how a trapping field acts on both clock levels, and it removed the reason that neutral-atom clocks were thought unable to compete with a single ion. That is a change in what is possible, not just a better build. I also note that Mehlig's own hesitation on B016 is attribution: the choice between Mele and Hasan, and the omission of Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang, is something we cannot resolve by scientific argument. If the committee wants a two-name prize with no arbitrary exclusion within the credited set, B059 provides it. I will not argue that B016 is a weaker discovery; my claim is that it is the harder prize to award fairly this year.

responses.point: Olsson calls B059 the best-attributed candidate and the strongest competitor to B016, but says topological insulators already changed how a whole class of materials is understood while the clock payoff is partly prospective; she adds she would not object to B059.
responses.response: I agree with most of this, and the point about prospective payoff is one I had already conceded. I would only separate two things. The redefinition of the second is prospective; the 1e-18 accuracy, the independent reproduction and the clock-comparison results are not, and that is where I place the weight. On breadth, I think the case that topological insulators changed how condensed-matter physicists classify materials is correct and I would not dispute it. The question we should put to ourselves is whether the Nobel criterion is breadth of conceptual change or the size of the discovery within its own field. Within precision measurement, the lattice clock is the step that moved optical clocks from a few ions to ensembles, and I would not call that incremental from where I work. I also take her point that the Hall-Haensch prize covered the comb; the citation should therefore not mention frequency metrology generally.

responses.point: Eriksson moved to B016, regards B059 as having the cleanest attribution but as less transformative for the broader physics community, and says the precision and attribution arguments do not by themselves place it above B016.
responses.response: I agree that precision and attribution alone are not sufficient, and I do not want to win on those two points. The broader-impact argument is where we disagree, and I think it cuts less cleanly than it first appears. The clocks are now used by people outside atomic physics: for relativistic geodesy, for searches for variation of constants and dark-matter signatures, and as the reference for comparing time across continents. That is a measurement capability reaching other fields, which is the form of influence I would expect from this kind of work, whereas the topological classification influences electronic-structure searches mainly in condensed matter. I would not call either broader in an absolute sense. My concern with B016 remains that Eriksson himself lists the omission of Hasan and Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang as the principal weakness; a three-person limit would make that omission a visible part of the prize.

responses.point: Pearce, now supporting B059, warns that the citation must name the lattice clock and its accuracy and not frequency metrology generally, or the overlap objection becomes serious, and shares unease about weighing Ye against NIST/JILA and European groups.
responses.response: I agree on the citation and have changed the wording to say what is distinctive: magic-wavelength trapping and parallel interrogation of many neutral atoms. On Ye versus the wider JILA/NIST community I share the unease, and I should be explicit that Ye's name stands for a group effort in a way that Katori's does not. I still keep Ye in the pair, because the 1e-18 stability and accuracy results and the many-body clock work are most closely associated with his laboratory in the supplied evidence, and because the alternative of a larger list would be arbitrary. I would not call it a perfect assignment, and I would ask the committee to state in the explanatory text that other groups reproduced and extended the result.

responses.point: Johansson says the lattice clock is largely a better realisation of a recognised idea, would accept it as a second-tier option, and does not think it clearly outranks a candidate that opened a new platform for quantum information.
responses.response: I do not accept that the lattice clock is simply a better realisation of the ion-clock idea. A single ion has one particle's worth of signal, and a neutral-atom ensemble trapped in an optical lattice changes the scaling of the problem, provided the trap-induced shift can be cancelled, which is what the magic wavelength does. That is why the 2012 prize does not pre-empt it. On circuit QED I still see closeness to the 2025 prize as a reason to wait, and I note that Johansson's own disclosure and the omission of Girvin add complications that B059 does not have; my first-round view that B013 is a strong later candidate stands, but I would not support it ahead of B059 this year.

responses.point: Lindroth asks that the distinction between parallel many-atom interrogation and the 2005 and 2012 recognitions be checked against the primary literature and not only recollection.
responses.response: That is fair, and I should say plainly that my answer to the chair rests on my own knowledge of the field and not on a fresh check of the papers. The points I would want confirmed before a final vote are the dates of Katori's proposal and the first lattice-clock measurements, and the origin of the 1e-18 uncertainty budgets. I do not expect these to change the two-name configuration, but I would not want the committee to rely on our recollection alone for the citation text.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the lattice clock as different in kind from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize, or sees it as a refinement; I think it is different in kind but I am an interested reader of this literature.
Whether Ye's name adequately stands for the wider JILA/NIST work, and whether Lemonde or another group has a distinct conceptual contribution; I have not found one and I cannot settle it from memory.

The priority chronology of Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and the first lattice-clock results, and the detailed history of the 1e-18 milestone, which I have not verified against the primary papers.
Whether waiting for the redefinition of the second would be wiser; I do not think so, because the case stands on demonstrated accuracy.
Whether B016 is a greater scientific advance than B059; I do not claim that it is not, only that its attribution is harder to defend.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure: I spent a research stay in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder during my doctoral period, and Hall is associated with the frequency-comb work on which the Ye group builds. I have no documented collaboration with Katori or Ye. I work in atomic physics and laser spectroscopy generally, which biases me toward precision measurement, and my opening and round-1 first place for B059 should be read with that in mind. After the round-1 discussion I do not think this requires recusal, but I leave that judgement to the chair and the committee, and I will accept a recusal on B059 if the committee prefers it.
